name: Kyoto
info: Kyoto is a city in the Yamashiro Basin on Honshu, Japan, founded in 794 as Heian-kyō, the seat of the imperial court for more than a thousand years, and now the capital of Kyoto Prefecture.

facts.founded: Chosen in 794 by Emperor Kanmu as the new seat of the imperial court and laid out as Heian-kyō on the model of the Tang capital Chang'an; the Shimogamo Shrine is believed to date from the 6th century.
facts.where: In the Yamashiro (Kyoto) Basin, ringed by hills on three sides, between the Kamo, Katsura and Uji rivers, on Honshu in the Kansai region of Japan.
facts.known: Heian-kyō, the imperial capital from 794; the Ōnin War; the Muromachi shogunate; Hideyoshi's rebuilding of the streets; Nijō Castle; about 2,000 temples and shrines; kimono weaving; the Gion Matsuri
facts.today: Kyoto is the capital of Kyoto Prefecture in the Kansai region, with about one and a half million people.

t: Kyoto began in 794 when Emperor Kanmu moved the court from Nara to Heian-kyō, a grid city modelled on Chang'an, and it remained the capital until the court moved to Tokyo in 1869.
Military rulers governed from Kamakura and Edo and, in the Muromachi period, from Kyoto itself, but the city stayed the seat of the emperors, and it was rebuilt after the Ōnin War of 1467–1477.
After the capital moved Kyoto built a canal, electric power and a modern municipality, and it was removed from the list of atomic bomb targets, so that much of its older building survives.
dyk: Japan's first electric tram line ran in Kyoto, made possible by the Lake Biwa Canal, which supplied hydroelectric power from 1895.
ev: The Shimogamo Shrine is believed to have been established in the area

sections.origins:
Archaeological evidence suggests that people lived in the area of Kyoto as early as the Palaeolithic period, although little has been published about human activity there before the 6th century, around which time the Shimogamo Shrine is believed to have been established. Immigrants from mainland Asia contributed to the development of the area before it became the imperial capital.

The site is a valley in the Yamashiro Basin, in the eastern part of the Tamba highlands. Hills known as Higashiyama, Kitayama and Nishiyama enclose it on three sides, rising to about 1,000 metres, and three rivers cross the basin: the Uji to the south, the Katsura to the west and the Kamo to the east. The city stands on a large natural water table that supplies it with wells.

In the 8th century powerful Buddhist clergy became involved in the affairs of the imperial government, and Emperor Kanmu chose to move the capital to distance it from the clerical establishment in Nara. His last choice of site was the village of Uda, in the Kadono district of Yamashiro Province. The new city, Heian-kyō, meaning 'tranquillity and peace capital', became the seat of the imperial court in 794 and began the Heian period. It was modelled on the Tang capital Chang'an and arranged in accordance with Chinese feng shui, with the palace facing south, so that the left sector, Sakyō, lay to the east and the right, Ukyō, to the west.
sections.growth:
The Heian period lasted from 794 to 1185. Late in it the city came to be called simply Kyōto, 'capital city', rather than Heian-kyō. Military rulers set up their governments in Kyoto itself under the Muromachi shogunate, or elsewhere, in Kamakura and Edo, yet Kyoto stayed the capital. It was the largest city in Japan until the late 16th century, when Osaka and Edo overtook it.

After the Ōnin War Toyotomi Hideyoshi rebuilt the city in the late 16th century. He laid out new streets that doubled the number of north–south streets in central Kyoto, which made rectangular blocks in place of the ancient square ones, and he built earthwork walls called odoi round it. He also gathered temples along Teramachi Street, which remains a Buddhist temple quarter. Under the Tokugawa shogunate, set up at Edo in 1603, Kyoto flourished as one of the three major cities of Japan with Osaka and Edo.

When the emperor moved to Tokyo in 1869 the city's economic and administrative standing was threatened, and the city government and local interests set out to strengthen its industry. Construction of the Lake Biwa Canal began in 1885 and was completed on 9 April 1890. The 20 kilometre waterway brought drinking water and irrigation and, from 1895, hydroelectric power for factories and street lighting, and it made possible Japan's first electric tram line. The city took in Fushimi, Kii, Kadono and Otagi in 1918 and 1931, and by 1932 its population exceeded one million.
sections.rulers:
Kyoto was the seat of the emperors from 794 until 1869, when the court moved to Tokyo. The Heian period ended in 1185. After it, military rulers held power by their own governments: the Muromachi shogunate in Kyoto, the Kamakura shogunate at Kamakura and the Tokugawa shogunate at Edo, where it was established in 1603, yet Kyoto remained the capital.

The Tokugawa shoguns built much of Nijō Castle in Kyoto, now among the city's World Heritage monuments. Toyotomi Hideyoshi remade the city's streets in the late 16th century. In 1864 the Hamaguri rebellion burned 28,000 houses, which showed the rebels' dissatisfaction with the Tokugawa shogunate, and the Boshin War included the Battle of Toba–Fushimi, one of the key events that took place in the city.

After the Meiji Restoration the capital was relocated to Tokyo, and for a short time Kyoto was called Saikyō, 'western capital'. The modern municipality of Kyoto was established in 1889.
sections.life:
The streets of the old city follow the grid of Heian-kyō, and the inner city was known as rakuchū and the suburbs beyond it as rakugai. Traditional townhouses called machiya survive in numbers because the city was spared in the Second World War.

Kyoto holds roughly 2,000 religious places, 1,600 Buddhist temples and 400 Shinto shrines, together with palaces and gardens. The Kyoto Gyoen area holds the Kyoto Imperial Palace and the Sentō Imperial Palace, homes of the emperors for many centuries, and the Katsura and Shugakuin imperial villas stand elsewhere in the city. Until the late Edo period the Kyoto dialect, Kyō-kotoba, was the de facto standard Japanese. Kimono weaving and sake brewing are named as traditional industries that remain.

The city's festivals are said to have been held for over 1,000 years: the Aoi Matsuri on 15 May, the Gion Matsuri, one of the three great festivals of Japan, whose parade is held on 17 July, the Gozan no Okuribi on 16 August, when fires lit on mountains guide the spirits home, and the Jidai Matsuri, the Festival of the Ages, on 22 October.
sections.crises:
The Ōnin War of 1467–1477 caused the city's worst destruction. Battles between samurai factions spilled into the streets and came to involve the court nobility, the kuge, and religious factions. Nobles' mansions were turned into fortresses, deep trenches were dug across the city for defence and as firebreaks, and numerous buildings burned. The city did not really recover until the middle of the 16th century and has not seen such widespread destruction since. The Honnō-ji Incident and the Kinmon incident also took place in Kyoto.

The Hamaguri rebellion of 1864 burned down 28,000 houses. The Battle of Toba–Fushimi of the Boshin War was fought at the city, and when the emperor left in 1869 the city's standing was threatened. Kyoto was ravaged by wars, fires and earthquakes during its eleven centuries as the imperial capital.

At the end of the Second World War the United States considered Kyoto as a target for an atomic bomb, because the city's importance was thought great enough that its loss might persuade Japan to surrender. At the insistence of Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of War in the Roosevelt and Truman administrations, it was removed from the list of targets and replaced by Nagasaki. The city was also largely spared conventional bombing, although small air raids caused casualties. During the occupation the US Sixth Army and I Corps were headquartered there.
sections.legacy:
Kyoto is regarded as the cultural capital of Japan. About 20% of the country's National Treasures and 14% of its Important Cultural Properties are in the city. In 1994 seventeen monuments were inscribed as the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto, among them the Kamo Shrines, Tō-ji, Kiyomizu-dera, Daigo-ji, Ninna-ji, Saihō-ji, Tenryū-ji, Rokuon-ji (Kinkaku-ji), Jishō-ji (Ginkaku-ji), Ryōan-ji, Hongan-ji, Kōzan-ji and Nijō Castle. Kiyomizu-dera is a wooden temple supported by pillars off the slope of a mountain, Kinkaku-ji is the Temple of the Golden Pavilion, Ginkaku-ji the Temple of the Silver Pavilion, and Ryōan-ji has a rock garden.

The Heian Jingū, a Shinto shrine built in 1895, commemorates the first and last emperors to reside in Kyoto, and the temple of Sennyū-ji holds the tombs of the emperors from Shijō to Kōmei.

The abundance of prewar buildings is unusual among Japanese cities, although modernisation continues to replace traditional Kyoto with newer architecture such as the Kyōto Station complex. Kyoto is now the capital of Kyoto Prefecture, in the Kansai region, with about one and a half million people.

summary: Kyoto was founded in 794 as Heian-kyō and was the seat of Japan's imperial court until the court moved to Tokyo in 1869. It was rebuilt after the Ōnin War, built a canal and electric power after losing the capital, and was spared large-scale destruction in the Second World War, so that many older buildings remain.
notes: The article on Kyoto is thin on history: it has no section on the Heian period itself, the Kamakura or Muromachi shogunates, Nijō Castle (named only among the World Heritage monuments, as 'primarily built by the Tokugawa shōguns'), or 1868. I wrote only what it supports and did not pad.

Dates for the end of the capital: the article says 'from 794 to 1868' (Etymology), 'until 1869' (lead and Origins) and 'the transfer of the imperial court to Tokyo in 1869'. I give 1869 for the move and mention the discrepancy in the rulers section.
The article lists the Hamaguri rebellion of 1864 and the Kinmon incident separately; it does not say whether they are one event, so I did not equate them.
The article names the model as 'Chang'an' in the lead and Origins and 'Chang'an/Luoyang' in Cityscape; I used Chang'an.

The article does not say why Stimson insisted on removing Kyoto from the target list, only that he did and that Nagasaki replaced it. The reason I gave (importance great enough that its loss might persuade Japan to surrender) is the article's reason for the US considering Kyoto a target, not for removing it.

Left out because not in the article: the Heian court's culture, the Kamakura period, details of the Muromachi shogunate, the Honnō-ji Incident's events, Nijō Castle's construction date, and anything about 1868 itself or the Meiji court's move beyond the year.

'Festivals held for over 1,000 years' is the article's own claim, hedged here as 'said to have been'. 'Fires and earthquakes' is the article's phrase, with no dates. The 'Hamaguri rebellion' sentence follows the article's reading ('which showed the rebels' dissatisfaction').
